ai.literal: They who love, by those they love to be loved having obtained, have obtained indeed, love's seedless fruit.
ai.translation: Those who are loved in return by the very ones they love have truly obtained the seedless, sweet fruit of love.
ai.modern: தாங்கள் விரும்புகின்ற காதலரால் தங்களையும் விரும்பப் பெற்றவர்கள், காமத்தின் விதையற்ற இனிமையான கனியைப் பெற்றவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the rare joy of mutual love. The speaker explains that when a person is loved back by the one they desire, they experience the ultimate fulfillment of love. This perfect union is compared to a seedless fruit (காழில் கனி). In a fruit, the hard seed or stone (காழ்) represents bitterness, pain, or difficulty, so a seedless fruit represents pure, uninterrupted sweetness and pleasure without any distress.

ai.literal: To those who live, like what the sky yielded indeed, to those who love, is the affection that the beloved bestow.
ai.translation: Just as the rain from the sky sustains those who live on earth, the affection bestowed by the beloved sustains those who love them.
ai.modern: வாழும் மக்களுக்கு வானம் மழை பொழிந்து உதவுவது போல, காதலிப்பவர்களுக்கு அவர்கள் காதலிப்பவர் காட்டும் அன்பானது அமைகிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the life-giving nature of rain to the sustaining power of a beloved's affection. For those who live in the world, the rain from the sky (வானம்) is essential for survival, yielding (பயந்து) timely sustenance. Similarly, for those who are deeply in love (வீழ்வார்க்கு), the grace and affection (அளி) bestowed by their beloved (வீழ்வார்) is the very source of their life. Without the beloved's love, the lover cannot survive, just as the world cannot survive without rain.

ai.literal: To those who are loved by those who love them, is indeed fitting the pride of saying 'we shall live'.
ai.translation: Only to those who are loved in return by those they love does the proud confidence of saying 'we shall live' belong.
ai.modern: தம்மை விரும்புபவர்களால் தாமும் விரும்பப்படும் பேறு பெற்றவர்களுக்கே, 'நாம் இன்பமாக வாழ்வோம்' என்னும் பெருமிதம் பொருந்தும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the necessity of mutual affection in love. The speaker observes that the proud confidence of declaring 'we shall live happily' (வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு) belongs only to those who are loved back by their partners (வீழப் படுவார்க்கு). The word 'செருக்கு' here represents the joyful security and self-assurance born of reciprocal love. Without this mutual bond, the separation becomes unbearable, and the hope of life fades away.

ai.literal: Those who are loved have no close intimacy, if those whom they themselves love do not love them in return.
ai.translation: Those who are loved by others have no real happiness if the ones they themselves love do not love them in return.
ai.modern: தாம் விரும்புகின்றவர் தம்மை விரும்பவில்லை என்றால், பிறரால் விரும்பப்படும் பெருமையைப் பெற்றிருந்தாலும் அவர்கள் உண்மையான அன்பின் இன்பத்தைப் பெறாதவர்களே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the deep sorrow of unrequited love. The speaker points out that even if a person is highly desired or loved by others ('வீழப் படுவார்'), they do not possess the true blessing of mutual intimacy ('கெழீஇயிலர்') if the specific person they desire does not return that love ('தாம்வீழ்வார் வீழப் படாஅர் எனின்'). The word 'கெழீஇ' denotes a close, fortunate bond of affection, which remains empty ('இலர்') without reciprocity. True fulfillment in love is not about being loved in general, but about being loved by the one you love.

ai.literal: We love those who held, to us what benefit will they do, they themselves love not having when?
ai.translation: What can the one whom we love do for us, if he himself does not feel love for us?
ai.modern: நாம் அன்பு செலுத்தும் காதலர், அவராக நம்மிடம் அன்பு செலுத்தாதபோது, நமக்கு என்ன செய்ய முடியும்?
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the pining lover laments the futility of one-sided love. The phrase 'nām kātal koṇṭār' refers to the beloved whom the speaker loves. The word 'kaṭai' is used here as a conditional term meaning 'when' or 'if'. The speaker asks what help or comfort ('evaṉ') the beloved can possibly offer ('ceypavō') if they themselves ('tām') do not feel any love ('kātal koḷḷā') in return. It beautifully captures the helplessness of loving someone who remains indifferent.

ai.literal: One-sidedly is painful love, carrying pole like, on both sides also is sweet.
ai.translation: Love is painful when it is one-sided; like a carrying pole, it is sweet only when balanced on both sides.
ai.modern: காவடித் தண்டு இரு பக்கமும் சமமாக இருந்தால் தான் சுமக்க இனிமையாக இருக்கும்; அதுபோல, காதலும் இரு பக்கமும் இருந்தால் தான் இன்பம் தரும், ஒரு பக்கமாக மட்டும் இருந்தால் துன்பம் தரும்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the poet compares love to a carrying pole ('கா'), which is used to carry loads balanced on both ends. If a carrying pole is loaded on only one side ('ஒருதலையான்'), it becomes unbalanced and painful ('இன்னாது') to carry. Similarly, love that is one-sided brings only grief and suffering to the person who feels it. Love becomes sweet ('இனிது') and harmonious only when it is mutual and shared equally by both partners ('இருதலையானும்'), just like a perfectly balanced carrying pole.

ai.literal: Affliction and sorrow, does he not see, Kama, who abides and acts upon only one person?
ai.translation: Does the god of love, who persists in tormenting only one of us, not see the affliction and sorrow that I suffer?
ai.modern: ஒருவரிடம் மட்டுமே நிலைத்து நின்று செயல்படும் காமன், எனது துன்பத்தையும் வருத்தத்தையும் பார்க்க மாட்டானோ?
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine laments her solitary suffering in separation. She wonders if Kama, the god of love, is blind to her intense distress. She uses the phrase 'oruvaṟkaṇ niṉṟoḻukuvāṉ' (one who abides and acts upon only one person) to point out the unfairness of her situation. Love should affect both partners equally, yet she feels that Kama has targeted only her, leaving her to bear the twin burdens of affliction ('paruvaral') and sorrow ('paital') alone.

ai.literal: Than those who love sweet words without receiving, in the world, than those who live, hard-hearted people there is none.
ai.translation: There are no people in this world more hard-hearted than those who continue to live even without receiving sweet words of comfort from their beloved.
ai.modern: தங்களை விரும்புபவரிடமிருந்து இனிய சொற்களைப் பெறாமல், இந்த உலகத்தில் உயிர் வாழ்கின்றவர்களைப் போல வன்நெஞ்சம் உடையவர்கள் வேறு யாரும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the pining heroine speaks of her own state of survival during separation. She laments that she is still alive despite not hearing any sweet, comforting words from her beloved. By calling those who survive such grief 'வன்கணார்' (hard-hearted or stubborn ones), she mockingly accuses herself of having an incredibly tough, unyielding heart that refuses to break and let her die, highlighting the sheer intensity of her solitary suffering.

ai.explanation: The heroine, suffering from the pain of separation, expresses her deep love. Even though her beloved does not return to show his grace (nalkār), any sound, word, or news (icai) coming from him or concerning him is sweet to her ears. The word 'icai' here refers to the sound of his name or news about him. This shows that for a true lover, even the mere mention of the beloved brings comfort, despite their painful absence.

ai.literal: To the one who does not love, intense pain you speak; the ocean you do not dry up; may you live, O heart!
ai.translation: May you prosper, my heart! You reveal your deep torment to him who does not love you; why do you not rather try to dry up the roaring ocean that torments me?
ai.modern: என் நெஞ்சே! நீ வாழ்க! உன்னிடம் அன்பு காட்டாதவரிடம் உன்னுடைய மிகுந்த துன்பத்தைச் சொல்கிறாய்; அதற்குப் பதிலாக, உன்னைத் துன்புறுத்தும் இந்தக் கடலை வற்றச் செய்யாமல் இருக்கிறாயே!
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine addresses her own heart in deep distress. She notes that her heart keeps yearning for and trying to communicate its intense suffering to her beloved, who remains indifferent and does not return her love. She sarcastically blesses her heart and suggests that trying to dry up the vast, roaring ocean—which worsens her grief with its relentless sound—would be just as futile, yet perhaps a better task than pleading with an unfeeling lover. The word 'செறாஅஅய்' is used here in the sense of drying up or scooping out the ocean, highlighting the impossibility and desperation of her situation.
